From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1733. Batavia. To His Excellency, a Most Noble and Esteemed Lord, Mr. Dirk van Cloon, Governor General, and the Noble Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Most Noble and Esteemed, Great and Honored: Earnest, Valiant, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords.

Received on the 25th of May 1733.

After we had obtained our orders from Your Excellency's Great Honor, we departed on the 9th of March last with the ship Westerbeek [ship name] under sail, in the company of the yacht De Vriendschap [The Friendship], and the Tanjongvouren, the Onbeschaamtheid [The Shamelessness], and the Kranke [The Sick], which arrived together with us on the 22nd of that date before the river of Banjarmasin, which we first sailed up with those small boats and arrived before the village of Tatas on the 26th of the same month. The letter and gift goods which Your Excellency's Great Honor had directed for the Sultan Akomoddin, we delivered on the 21st of March while presenting Your Excellency's Great Honor's most amiable greetings to that prince, though no business matters were handled at that time. But upon a later audience with that Majesty concerning the pepper trade, since a great quantity was in readiness in the surrounding villages, which we requested and would be delivered to the Company alone, the king did not seem to dare to express his true meaning clearly, but gave only ambiguous answers and we could discern nothing to secure the trade. Therefore we betook ourselves to Pangeran Praboe Anum, to whom we proposed Your Excellency's Great Honor's meaning in earnest terms regarding pepper alone, who answered us somewhat reluctantly that two wankangs [type of vessel] or junks must be loaded alongside, and the Company's ship shall also be provided with pepper. The yacht De Vriendschap and 24 pieces of muskets for the account of this prince were also brought,

On the occasion when we had the honor of giving a visit to the Sultan Akomoddin and Pangeran Praboe Anum, by virtue of which we made known to them that Your Excellency's Great Honor had ordered us to form new contracts with our friends, should they be inclined thereto, and to grant the Company alone the pepper trade here, His Majesty answered us that he would for now hold to the contracts made with the previous Panabahan and yearly when junks came here, they must be tolerated for that trade, and also that they were in a position to have consulted with the further regents of this realm before answering us, which we are still awaiting to this day. From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1733. We have been brought 70,000 pounds

We have been informed here from the side that the pepper crop of the previous year has been very good, for in the uplands and the surrounding villages there is well 15,000 picols in stock, of which we shall obtain the smallest quantity to our sorrow. We have been brought 70,000 pounds of pepper which have been loaded in the ship Westerbeek, and now most of the Chinese and native merchants are bringing that Chinese junk which we found here before Tatas upon our arrival, which will be able to depart from here with a quantity of 12 to 13,000 picols, which will considerably reduce the stock, and it is to be feared that the ship Westerbeek will not be able to obtain a full cargo within two or three months. The pepper harvest of this year stands to this day in poor condition due to the continuing rain that has fallen here, and it is thought that little of that green pepper of this monsoon will be able to be obtained, which we leave to the wiser judgment of Your Excellency's Great Honor whether such can be relied upon, to prevent the great losses that could be caused by the delivery of goods again. Regarding the two pepper scales which were also given by Your Excellency's Great Honor for the weighing of that pepper, they are of no use here, although we have sought to obtain such through earnest and persistent requests to the king and prince, it has been fruitless. The same was true for obtaining a proper result on each weighing, which has compelled us to store those goods dry and unscraped, in hope of a generous accommodation and approval of Your Excellency's

The same was true for obtaining a proper result on each weighing, which has compelled us to store those goods dry and unscraped, in hope of a generous accommodation and approval of Your Excellency's Great Honor. We have until now not been able to discern that the king and prince are well disposed toward the Company, for they prefer to sell their goods to foreign merchants rather than to the Company, which is evident from the fact that previously they always had a proclamation circulated to make known to the inhabitants that their pepper would be delivered to the Company alone. From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1733. This has not yet occurred to this day, which is indeed a principal reason why we have collected so little pepper until now and our fear is that in this monsoon not more than one ship's cargo of dry pepper will be able to be obtained. The officers of the ship Westerbeek have properly delivered their cargo, except that in case number 40, in which were enclosed 24 pieces of muskets, we found only 23 pieces, and since those firearms were destined for the account of the Sultan, we have taken one firearm from that hold to make up for the shortage, of which we hope to obtain a favorable approval from Your Excellency's Great Honor, whose pious and weighty concerns we in all holy reverence have commended. We remain with deep respect, Most Noble, Esteemed, and Widely Commanding Lords, Your High Excellency's obedient and humble servants. [Signed] C. De Marre and D. Brouwer. From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1733. Banjarmasin in the village Tatas.

The 2nd of May, in the Year 1733. Batavia. To His Excellency, Most Noble and Esteemed Lord Dirk van Cloon, Governor General, and the Noble Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Most Noble and Esteemed, Great and Honored: Earnest, Valiant, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords.

Our humble letters of the 2nd of the past month of May we hope will have been received well by Your High Excellency, of which this is a duplicate, wherein we have communicated to Your High Excellency's Great Honor that we had purchased 50,000 pounds of pepper, which quantity has only been increased to 172,012 pounds, which we have obtained with much effort and continual requests to the Sultan, Pangeran, and those who are appointed for this purpose in this village, from one another. Of these, two of the three Chinese junks have been fully loaded and have already departed, the last shall also undertake its journey within a few days.

From Banjarmasin, the 2nd of May 1723. Brouwer /in margin/ Banjarmasin in the Negeri Tatas, the 2nd of May, Year 1723.— Batavia. To His Excellency, the Most Esteemed, High and Noble, Strict Lord Dirk van Cloon, Governor General, and the Noble Lords, Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Most High and Noble, Strict, Great and Esteemed, Earnest, Faithful, Wise, Prudent, and Most Generous Lords. We hope that our humble letters of the 2nd of the past month of May will have been received well by Your High Excellencies, of which this is a duplicate, wherein we have communicated to Your High Excellencies that we had purchased 50,000 pounds of pepper, which quantity has only increased to 172,012 pounds, which we have obtained with much effort and continual requests from the Sultan, the Pangeran, and those appointed in this negeri [settlement], whereby two of the three Chinese junks have been fully loaded and have already departed, the last one shall also undertake its journey within a few days. Banjarmasin, the 11th of June 1733. Regarding the pepper trade for the Esteemed Company, to have it exclusively from these lands, we regard as an impossible matter, for although the Sultan and Prince Praboe Anum keep us occupied with promises and provide assurances in their letters to Your High Excellencies, their powers in execution do not prove sufficient, partly due to the disloyalty of their trusted servants, who allow themselves to be easily corrupted, and on the other hand, the enmity in which the princes commonly live, and those who will not observe any order from the king, and brings then, on account of the higher price that the Chinese pay for pepper, their goods to the same, which gives a foothold so that the common subjects follow, imagining themselves just as well as a pangeran [prince] to be able to transgress the orders, for which no punishment is administered,

--- CHUNK 2 ---
servants who allow themselves to be easily corrupted, and on the other hand, the enmity in which the princes commonly live, and those who will not observe any order from the king, and brings then, on account of the higher price that the Chinese pay for pepper, their goods to the same, which gives a foothold so that the common subjects follow, imagining themselves just as well as a pangeran to be able to transgress the orders, for which no punishment is administered, as we have seen when the king had the proclamation made and announced around, that each one should bring his pepper to the Esteemed Company on pain of confiscation of goods, but since that time the Chinese received in greater quantities than before; and to Banjarmasin, the 11th of June 1733, we were brought thirty to thirty-five baskets of pepper every two or three days, besides which mandarin vessels have approached before and in this river, which we cannot fail to communicate to Your High Excellencies, they have brought a letter with a horse and an extraordinarily large clappus [gift/tribute] for this prince as a gift, and a claim of 2,000 Spanish reals [modern equivalent: approximately 2,000 silver coins], which the same demands from this king, who denies owing no money to the mandarins, we are informed from this side that this claim of money would only be to have an arrival here, and upon non-payment to see themselves avenged for the injustice done a year ago by the peoples of Pangeran Manko Nagara, with the murder of several great ones in their negeri, many vessels are also being prepared here, some of which have already been driven to Old Banjarmasin to be able to attack the mandarins when they wish to use hostilities, but as we were informed, those peoples are afraid of the ship of the Esteemed Company. From Banjarmasin, the 11th of June 1733, of the king

From Banjarmasin, the 11th of June 1733, of the king. This prince's great lack of money is the reason he has demanded from us 500 Spanish reals, the payment of which we requested might be delayed a little longer, until somewhat more pepper had been collected, for today the Sultan's debt was not possible to make greater, as we are already fearful that the toll of the pepper will not amount to as much as the king of Banjarmasin, the 1st of June 1723, owes to the Esteemed Company, for which reason we shall give no money for His Majesty's account with the Esteemed Company is settled. From Banjarmasin, the 11th of June 1733. We have endeavored to observe Your High Excellencies' honored commands in all respects and principally to encourage the king and Pangeran Praboe Anum to obtain a strong quantity of pepper, but we find from the aforementioned reasons that all is fruitless, for to the loading of the ship Westerbeek, so much pepper shall not be obtainable from this baijboen [uncertain: possibly a place name] as that vessel could carry from here, because the junks have purchased that cargo master, and the crop now standing in the field promises very little, for which reason we are obliged to communicate to Your High Excellencies that the provisions for the peoples on the ship Westerbeek lying here at the roadstead are beginning to diminish considerably, and by the 9th of August, the same

For the loading of the ship Westerbeek, we shall not be able to obtain as much pepper from this region as that vessel could carry from here, because the Junks whose Corlmeest [uncertain: possibly a title or position] have purchased it, and the crop currently standing in the field promises very little. Therefore, we are greatly obliged to inform your High Excellency that the provisions for the people on the ship Westerbeek lying here at the roadstead are beginning to diminish considerably and by the 9th of August will only be sufficient for that long. Therefore our request is that your High Excellency might be pleased to provision that vessel with more supplies for as many months as shall be agreeable to your High Excellency's judgment. We shall keep that ship here, and our humble petition to your High Excellency is that we may be favored with the much honored order to depart with the Janjermassing on the 11th of June 1733 from this region in a coastal direction, as the westerly monsoon will not be favorable for us here. We beseech a favorable consideration from your High Excellency. We have not brought to the attention of your High Excellency in our previous letters that 50 pounds of gunpowder for the account of the Sultan were not shipped aboard the ship Westerbeek. Being in want of this from the aforementioned ship Westerbeek on multiple occasions, we have borrowed it, placed the Prince in our debt, and charged it according to the prices of previous years, for which we hope to obtain a favorable approval from your High Excellency. Regarding the Tanjongpoura, we had projected the shamelessness of bringing this to your High Excellency, but due to the arrival of the Mandarins, and as everything is still being prepared here for war, we have had to refrain from it. For when one of the small boats with pepper comes aboard, one would have someone in this territory to take our roadstead and retreat to the ship in case of any attack, although we have not yet been able to perceive any preparations for war other than what is being made for the Mandarins. Thus we have judged it best not to surrender ourselves entirely to the deceptive nature of these peoples, with which this concludes, having commended your High Excellency to God's holy care, we remain with great respect / [signature] And Lower [signature] as before / in margin /

From Banjarmasin, the 1st of June 1733. Extract from the Banjarmasin daily register, dated the 7th of June 1733. Toward evening one of the pepper writers came to tell us that Pangerang Prabanum wished to give us a visit at seven o'clock, which we granted to that Prince. We were of the opinion that he had an important reason to communicate it to us, because he had chosen such an inconvenient hour for it. That Prince appeared at the appointed time with a small retinue, as we had requested. We offered him tea, betel nut, and so forth. During this refreshment, that Prince asked us whether we wished to depart with the ship and Tanjongpoura soon. We answered that we would remain when pepper could be obtained in this territory. That Prince replied that there is little pepper left, and I fear that this year with the new pepper we shall not have more than the ship can load. He expressed to us that he is very much concerned for the Honored Company, and that he and the King would send a letter to the Governor-General in which they promised to deliver the pepper solely to the Honored Company. To this we replied that the Governor-General and the Council of India are qualified to make a contract with the King and all the Princes, excluding all others. And that when the King and Princes might resolve to do so, it must be stipulated that when anyone from this land wished to export pepper, the Honored Company would be free to seize it and confiscate it, or else divide it, one half for the King and the other half for the Honored Company. That Prince answered: I shall speak about this with the King, but I have not needed to involve the other Princes. We are now all good friends, and then the

That Prince answered: I shall speak about this with the King, but I have not needed to involve the other Princes. We are now all good friends, and then the other Princes will also bring their pepper to the Honored Company. We both think it better and also much more peaceful for the King and him, Pangerang, when all the Princes sign the contract together. For the King, living in enmity with some, would sometimes retract his word, whereas he, being otherwise persuaded, was to observe the contract even in enmity with the King. We requested that when the King consulted with all the Princes about this, we might be present, to assure all the state dignitaries of the good intentions of the Governor-General and the Council of India. That Prince answered that he would report one and another to the King. We requested that Prince to be so kind as to tell us what quantity of pepper, should the Honored Company obtain it alone, could be obtained here annually, and whether in other territories or at the foot of the mountains more pepper could not be cultivated to obtain a strong quantity annually. To this he answered us: Annually one ship full of pepper leaves this land. But previously there were four territories here named Pamanken, Caloa, Poain, and Mandit, where much pepper was cultivated, which today, because they lie underwater, are not accessible to it, and the mountains are also not suitable for the cultivation of that grain.

From Banjarmasin, the 1st of August 1733. High Noble, strict, greatly esteemed, most earnest, most wise, most prudent, and very generous lords. Our letters of the 11th of June of the previous year have, we trust, been delivered to your High Excellency in due time, whose duplicates extracted from the daily register of this [office] are enclosed herewith. And we have not without reason shared with your High Excellency our thoughts regarding a shortage of pepper to our regret in the previous letters, for with our last dispatch there was shipped in the ship Westerbeek 17,201½ pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 7,800 kg]. Since that time purchased 43,449 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 19,700 kg], so that the cargo loaded in the aforementioned vessel amounts to 245,461 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 111,300 kg] of pepper. What encouragement and requests we make to obtain a full cargo for the ship seems to be as fruitless with these people as our desire to fulfill [our goal] to speak with the Sultan in person, which under the pretext of one thing or another has been refused us on different occasions, and we have not been able to obtain vessels to undertake the journey to Cirebon and to achieve our objective. The second [letter] signed to Pangeran Marta Nagara on the 28th of the last month of July received on the 27th of August 1733. From Banjarmasin, the 10th of August 1733. A visit being made, he was received by the same with a kris at his side and a bare striped bale-bladed spear in his hand, and seemed more inclined to go away sorrowfully than to meet in a friendly manner, although nothing was accomplished thereby. Yet on his side that Pangeran remained [unmoved]. From Banjarmasin on the 29th of August 1733.— To Batavia. To His Excellency the highly noble and esteemed Lord Mr. Dirk van Illon, Governor General, and the noble gentlemen Councillors of the Dutch Indies. Highly noble, esteemed, great and worthy, earnest, steadfast, wise, prudent and most generous gentlemen.— Since our last respectful letters of the 10th of this month, whose duplicate is enclosed herewith, we have only been able to procure 17,929 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 8,100 kg] of pepper, which is a meager quantity at this time, whereas this commodity should now be brought in abundance, since the harvest from this past spring has already been delivered to the traders, who are unwilling to sell it for less than the price at which they purchased that grain during the time of the junks, and whereas our orders from your high Excellency are to spend 4 reals and a quarter [modern equivalent: a specific currency unit of the period] per picul [modern equivalent: approximately 61 kg], to which lower price the peoples here are not willing to travel to the aforementioned village to bring pepper from there, as they claim they can gain no advantage but must incur needless costs due to the high market prices. However, if the Sultan and Pangeran Praboe Anum now wish to demonstrate their zeal and goodwill toward the Esteemed Company, they would arrange matters and order the peoples of the aforementioned village to sell pepper as in previous years, and particularly as was done in 1727 and 1728, so that the transporters would be encouraged to make the journey, as was evident at that time, for then a considerable quantity was obtained. This matter we commend to your high Excellency in God's keeping, and take the liberty to name ourselves, with respect, your high Excellency's esteemed and widely commanding gentlemen. Your high Excellency's obedient and humble servants.
